concepts.name: States of matter and the kinetic particle theory
concepts.description: Properties of solids, liquids and gases; the arrangement, separation and motion of their particles; changes of state (melting, boiling, evaporating, freezing and condensing) explained by the kinetic particle theory in terms of energy and forces between particles; how temperature and pressure affect the volume of a gas (Cambridge Core describes, Supplement explains in terms of particles). ZIMSEC Form 3 states of matter.

concepts.name: Heating and cooling curves
concepts.description: Reading, sketching and interpreting heating and cooling curves; why the temperature stays constant while a substance melts, boils or freezes (energy is used to overcome, or is released by, the forces between particles); finding melting and boiling points from a curve; experiments such as heating ice or cooling stearic acid or naphthalene. Cambridge Supplement (1.1) and a practical-paper context; ZIMSEC Form 4. The effect of impurities is taught in chem.practical.purity.

concepts.name: Diffusion
concepts.description: Diffusion as the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration because of their random motion; diffusion in gases and liquids (potassium manganate(VII) crystals in water, perfume in a room, the ammonia and hydrogen chloride tube experiment); Cambridge Supplement: at the same temperature, gases with a lower relative molecular mass diffuse faster. ZIMSEC Form 3 (matter).

concepts.name: Elements, compounds and mixtures
concepts.description: Elements (made of one type of atom), compounds (two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion) and mixtures (substances not chemically combined); how they differ in composition, properties and how they can be separated; chemical symbols of elements; recognising elements, compounds and mixtures in particle diagrams. Cambridge 2.1; ZIMSEC Form 3 elements and compounds.

concepts.name: Physical and chemical changes
concepts.description: Telling physical changes (no new substance forms; usually easily reversed, such as melting or dissolving) from chemical changes (new substances form, often with a gas given off, a colour change, a precipitate or an energy change). Cambridge 6.1 only: ZIMSEC Forms 3-4 assume it from Forms 1-2 Combined Science.

concepts.name: Atomic structure
concepts.description: Protons, neutrons and electrons: where they are found in the atom and their relative charges and relative masses; proton (atomic) number and mass (nucleon) number; working out the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms and ions from nuclide notation (mass number top left, proton number bottom left). Cambridge 2.2; ZIMSEC Form 3 atomic structure and elements.

concepts.name: Electronic configuration
concepts.description: Arranging electrons in shells for atoms and ions of the elements with proton numbers 1 to 20, written as numbers (for example 2,8,3) and drawn as shell diagrams; links to the Periodic Table: outer-shell electrons equal the group number for Groups I to VII, the number of occupied shells equals the period number and the noble gases have full outer shells. Cambridge 2.2; ZIMSEC Form 3 (first 20 elements).

concepts.name: Isotopes
concepts.description: Isotopes as atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons; symbols for isotopes and ions; Cambridge Supplement: isotopes have the same chemical properties because they have the same electronic configuration, and relative atomic mass is calculated from isotope masses and abundances (for example chlorine-35 and chlorine-37). Cambridge 2.3; ZIMSEC Form 3 (the concept of an isotope).

concepts.name: Ionic bonding
concepts.description: Formation of positive ions (cations) and negative ions (anions) by electron transfer; the ionic bond as a strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; dot-and-cross diagrams (Cambridge Core: Group I with Group VII; Cambridge Supplement and ZIMSEC: other metal and non-metal compounds such as MgO, CaCl₂ and Al₂O₃); the giant ionic lattice (Supplement); properties of ionic compounds (high melting and boiling points, conduct when molten or dissolved but not when solid) and their explanation; telling ionic from covalent compounds by experiment.

concepts.name: Covalent bonding and simple molecules
concepts.description: Covalent bonds as shared pairs of electrons that give each atom a noble-gas configuration; single, double and triple bonds; dot-and-cross diagrams for H₂, Cl₂, H₂O, CH₄, NH₃ and HCl (Cambridge Core) and O₂, N₂, CO₂, C₂H₄ and CH₃OH (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC lists O₂, N₂ and CO₂); properties of simple molecular substances (low melting and boiling points because of weak forces between molecules, no electrical conductivity).

concepts.name: Giant covalent structures
concepts.description: The giant covalent structures of diamond and graphite and how they explain their properties and uses (graphite as a lubricant and as an electrode, diamond in cutting tools); Cambridge Supplement: the giant covalent structure of silicon(IV) oxide and its similarity to diamond. Cambridge 2.6; tagged to ZIMSEC covalent bonding (diamond and graphite are not named in the ZIMSEC matrix: reviewer to confirm).

concepts.name: Metallic bonding
concepts.description: Metallic bonding as the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive ions and a 'sea' of delocalised electrons, and how it explains the electrical and thermal conductivity, malleability and ductility of metals. Cambridge Supplement only (2.7); ZIMSEC Form 3.

concepts.name: Chemical formulae
concepts.description: Formulae of the elements and compounds met in the course; molecular and empirical formulae (definitions); deducing a formula from a model or diagram, including dot-and-cross diagrams; writing formulae of ionic compounds from ion charges or valencies, including compound ions (NH₄⁺, OH⁻, NO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻, CO₃²⁻); naming compounds, including Roman numerals for metals with more than one ion (iron(II), iron(III), copper(II)). Cambridge 3.1; ZIMSEC Form 3.

concepts.name: Word, symbol and ionic equations
concepts.description: Writing word equations and balanced symbol equations with state symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq); deducing the equation for a reaction from information given; Cambridge Supplement: ionic equations with spectator ions left out, for example for neutralisation, precipitation and displacement. Cambridge 3.1; ZIMSEC Form 3 chemical equations.

concepts.name: Relative atomic, molecular and formula masses
concepts.description: Relative atomic mass (Ar) as the average mass of an element's atoms compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; calculating relative molecular mass and relative formula mass (Mr) from a formula; Cambridge Core: reacting masses by simple proportion without the mole. Cambridge 3.2; ZIMSEC Form 3 mole concept.

concepts.name: The mole and the Avogadro constant
concepts.description: The mole as the amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles (the Avogadro constant); molar mass in g/mol; amount (mol) = mass (g) ÷ molar mass (g/mol) to find an amount, a mass, a molar mass or Ar/Mr; numbers of atoms, ions or molecules. Cambridge Supplement (3.3); ZIMSEC Form 3.

concepts.name: Reacting masses and limiting reactants
concepts.description: Using balanced equations and mole ratios to calculate the masses of reactants needed and products formed; identifying the limiting reactant and the reactant in excess, and the mass of product it limits. Cambridge Supplement (3.3); ZIMSEC Form 3 chemical equations (limiting reagents).

concepts.name: Molar gas volume
concepts.description: One mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.); converting between gas volume, amount and mass; volumes of gases reacting or produced in a reaction, including volume ratios from equations. Cambridge Supplement (3.3); ZIMSEC Form 4.

concepts.name: Concentration of solutions
concepts.description: Concentration in g/dm³ and mol/dm³ (Cambridge Core only states the units); converting volumes between cm³ and dm³; amount = concentration × volume; converting between g/dm³ and mol/dm³; the mass of solute needed to make a solution. Calculations are Cambridge Supplement (3.3); ZIMSEC Form 3 mole concept.

concepts.name: Titration calculations
concepts.description: Using titration results (the mean of concordant titres) and the balanced equation to calculate the amount of solute, an unknown concentration or the volume of solution needed, including mole ratios other than 1 : 1 and dilution steps. Cambridge Supplement (3.3); ZIMSEC Form 4 volumetric analysis. The practical technique is chem.practical.titration.

concepts.name: Percentage composition, empirical and molecular formulae
concepts.description: Percentage by mass of an element in a compound, including metals in ores (haematite, chalcopyrite (copper pyrites), bauxite) and nitrogen in fertilisers; calculating empirical formulae from masses or percentages and molecular formulae from the empirical formula and Mr. Cambridge Supplement (3.3); ZIMSEC Form 4 percentage composition.

concepts.name: Percentage yield and percentage purity
concepts.description: Theoretical yield, actual yield and percentage yield, and why actual yields are less than theoretical; percentage purity of a sample (for example impure limestone or an impure ore) from reacting masses or gas volumes. Cambridge Supplement (3.3); ZIMSEC Form 4.

concepts.name: Oxidation and reduction
concepts.description: Redox as oxidation and reduction happening together; oxidation and reduction as gain and loss of oxygen (Cambridge Core), as loss and gain of electrons and as an increase and decrease in oxidation number (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC Form 3); rules for oxidation numbers and Roman numerals in names; oxidising and reducing agents (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC Form 3); Cambridge Supplement: recognising redox with acidified potassium manganate(VII) (purple to colourless) and potassium iodide (colourless to brown).

concepts.name: Half-equations and redox equations
concepts.description: Writing ionic half-equations for oxidation and reduction, including reactions at electrodes, and combining them into balanced ionic redox equations (for example metal and halogen displacement reactions); identifying the species oxidised and reduced in an ionic equation. Cambridge Supplement (3.1, 4.1, 6.4); ZIMSEC Form 4 redox equations.

concepts.name: Electrolysis: principles and molten compounds
concepts.description: Electrolysis as the breaking down of an ionic compound, molten or in solution, by an electric current; anode (positive), cathode (negative), electrolyte and inert electrodes (carbon/graphite, platinum); why solid ionic compounds do not conduct; metals or hydrogen form at the cathode and non-metals at the anode; products of molten binary compounds such as lead(II) bromide; Cambridge Supplement: how charge moves (electrons in the external circuit, ions in the electrolyte) and electrode half-equations (oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode).

concepts.name: Electrolysis of aqueous solutions
concepts.description: Products and observations when solutions are electrolysed with inert electrodes: dilute sulfuric acid or acidified water (hydrogen and oxygen in a 2 : 1 volume ratio, which confirms the formula H₂O; uses of the gases: ZIMSEC Form 3) and concentrated aqueous sodium chloride (Cambridge Core); Cambridge Supplement: aqueous copper(II) sulfate with carbon and with copper electrodes, and predicting the products for dilute and concentrated halide solutions; tests for the gases formed.

concepts.name: Electroplating and the purification of copper
concepts.description: Electroplating (object as the cathode, plating metal as the anode, a solution of the plating metal's ions as the electrolyte) to improve appearance and resistance to corrosion; electrolytic purification of copper with an impure copper anode and a pure copper cathode in copper(II) sulfate solution, the anode slime and its valuable by-products; uses of copper. Cambridge 4.1 (copper electrodes are Supplement); ZIMSEC Form 4 electrolytic purification.

concepts.name: Simple cells and the lead-acid battery
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 3 only: a simple cell of two different metals in an electrolyte (zinc and copper in dilute acid or in a lemon); the electrode reactions; the further apart the metals are in the reactivity series, the larger the voltage; the lead-acid (car) battery: lead and lead(IV) oxide plates in sulfuric acid, discharging and recharging, and safe maintenance (topping up with distilled water, avoiding short circuits, handling the acid).

concepts.name: Hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells
concepts.description: Cambridge only (4.2): a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell uses hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity, with water as the only chemical product; Supplement: advantages and disadvantages compared with petrol engines in vehicles (no carbon dioxide at the point of use, efficiency; producing, storing and transporting hydrogen, cost).

concepts.name: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
concepts.description: Exothermic reactions transfer thermal energy to the surroundings (the temperature rises) and endothermic reactions take it in (the temperature falls); everyday and laboratory examples (burning fuels, neutralisation, dissolving ammonium nitrate, thermal decomposition, photosynthesis); bond breaking is endothermic and bond making exothermic, so the balance decides the overall change (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC Form 3); Cambridge Supplement: the enthalpy change ΔH is negative for exothermic and positive for endothermic reactions.

concepts.name: Reaction pathway (energy profile) diagrams
concepts.description: Interpreting (Cambridge Core) and drawing and labelling (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC Form 3) reaction pathway diagrams for exothermic and endothermic reactions, showing reactants, products, ΔH and the activation energy Ea; activation energy as the minimum energy colliding particles need to react; how a catalyst lowers the activation energy on the diagram.

concepts.name: Enthalpy changes from bond energies
concepts.description: Cambridge Supplement only (5.1): energy taken in to break the bonds in the reactants minus energy given out when the bonds in the products form; calculating ΔH from a table of bond energies using displayed formulae (for example burning methane, forming hydrogen chloride, the Haber reaction); deciding from the sign whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

concepts.name: Measuring enthalpy changes
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 4 only: measuring temperature changes to find enthalpy changes of combustion (spirit burner heating water in a calorimeter), neutralisation and solution (polystyrene cup); energy transferred q = mcΔT (specific heat capacity of water 4.2 J/g/°C; the mass of a dilute solution taken from its volume, 1 cm³ ≈ 1 g); ΔH per mole of fuel, water formed or solute; sources of error such as heat loss and incomplete combustion.

concepts.name: Factors affecting the rate of reaction
concepts.description: How concentration, gas pressure, surface area (particle size), temperature, stirring (ZIMSEC) and catalysts, including enzymes (catalase in potato or liver), change the rate of a reaction; a catalyst speeds up a reaction and is unchanged at the end (Cambridge Core); collision theory: particles per unit volume, collision frequency, particle energy and activation energy, used to explain each factor, and catalysts lowering the activation energy (Cambridge Supplement; expected in ZIMSEC explanations).

concepts.name: Measuring and interpreting rates of reaction
concepts.description: Practical methods: volume of gas against time (gas syringe or inverted measuring cylinder), loss in mass on a balance, time for a precipitate to hide a cross (sodium thiosulfate and acid) or for a colour change; plotting and interpreting rate graphs (steepest at the start, levelling off when a reactant is used up; comparing curves); calculating average rates from data and, for Cambridge Extended, from a tangent; Cambridge Supplement: evaluating methods. Cambridge 6.2; ZIMSEC Form 3.

concepts.name: Reversible reactions
concepts.description: Reactions that can go in both directions, shown by ⇌; changing the conditions changes the direction: heating hydrated copper(II) sulfate or cobalt(II) chloride and adding water to the anhydrous salts (Cambridge Core), and the chromate(VI)/dichromate(VI) change when acid or alkali is added (ZIMSEC Form 3).

concepts.name: Dynamic equilibrium and changing conditions
concepts.description: Dynamic equilibrium in a closed system: the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant; predicting and explaining how changing temperature, pressure or concentration shifts the position of equilibrium, and why a catalyst does not shift it (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC Form 3, for example iodine in a sealed tube).

concepts.name: The Haber process and ammonia
concepts.description: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g); nitrogen from the air and hydrogen from methane (Cambridge) or from the electrolysis of water (ZIMSEC links the process to electrolysis of water and the liquefaction of air); typical conditions 450 °C, 200 atm (20 000 kPa) and an iron catalyst; cooling to liquefy ammonia and recycling unreacted gases; uses of ammonia (fertilisers, nitric acid); ZIMSEC: safety and environmental impacts. Cambridge Supplement (6.3); ZIMSEC Form 3. Why these conditions are chosen is chem.industry.choosing-conditions.

concepts.name: The Contact process and sulfuric acid
concepts.description: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g); sulfur dioxide from burning sulfur or roasting sulfide ores, oxygen from air; typical conditions 450 °C, 2 atm (200 kPa) and a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst (Cambridge Supplement); ZIMSEC Form 3: the whole process including absorbing sulfur trioxide in concentrated sulfuric acid, uses of sulfuric acid (fertilisers, car batteries, detergents) and environmental impacts.

concepts.name: The Ostwald process and nitric acid
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 3 only: ammonia from the Haber process is oxidised by air over a platinum-rhodium catalyst to nitrogen monoxide, which forms nitrogen dioxide and is absorbed in water with more oxygen to make nitric acid; the conditions used; uses of nitric acid (ammonium nitrate fertiliser, explosives); hazards and environmental impacts (oxides of nitrogen).

concepts.name: Choosing industrial conditions
concepts.description: Explaining the typical conditions of the Haber and Contact processes as compromises between rate and equilibrium yield, energy and equipment costs and safety (Cambridge Supplement 6.3; ZIMSEC Form 4 industrial applications of reaction kinetics and equilibria); reading graphs of percentage yield against temperature and pressure; recycling unreacted gases; linking production costs to the cost of the product.

concepts.name: Fertilisers
concepts.description: Why plants need nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium; NPK fertilisers; ammonium salts and nitrates as fertilisers (Cambridge Core); ZIMSEC Form 4: making ammonium nitrate and ammonium sulfate by neutralising ammonia with nitric or sulfuric acid and crystallising (the syllabus suggests visits to Sable Chemicals and Zimphos); comparing fertilisers by percentage of nitrogen; problems caused by overuse.

concepts.name: Lime in agriculture and construction
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 3 only: making calcium oxide (quicklime) by heating calcium carbonate (limestone) in a lime kiln; slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) and limewater; using lime as a base to neutralise acidic soils and in construction (mortar, cement, whitewash); reactions of lime with acids.

concepts.name: Liquefaction and fractional distillation of air
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 4 only: the composition of air; removing water vapour and carbon dioxide, then compressing and cooling air until it liquefies; separating nitrogen, argon and oxygen by fractional distillation using their boiling points; uses of oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide and the noble gases (for example medical oxygen, welding and cutting, the Haber process, food packaging and freezing, fire extinguishers).

concepts.name: Processing coal and diamonds
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 4 only: processing coal (washing, coking by destructive distillation, coal gasification to carbon monoxide and hydrogen, and chemicals from coal tar) and diamonds (separating diamonds from ore by physical methods that use their high density and other properties, then cutting and polishing); value addition and beneficiation of these resources; environmental impacts, with Zimbabwean contexts such as the Hwange coalfield and the Marange diamond fields.

concepts.name: Properties of acids, bases and alkalis
concepts.description: Reactions of acids with metals, bases and carbonates (equations and observations); bases as metal oxides and hydroxides and alkalis as soluble bases; reactions of bases with acids and of alkalis with ammonium salts (ammonia released); acids contain H⁺(aq) and alkalis OH⁻(aq); neutralisation H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O; everyday acids and bases (vinegar, lemon juice, toothpaste, wood ash, lime). Cambridge 7.1; ZIMSEC Form 3.

concepts.name: Indicators and the pH scale
concepts.description: Colours of litmus, methyl orange and thymolphthalein in acids and alkalis (Cambridge); universal indicator and the pH scale (pH 7 neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 alkaline); comparing hydrogen ion concentration and how acidic or alkaline solutions are from colour and pH; indicators from plant extracts. Cambridge 7.1; ZIMSEC Form 3 (pH scale, acid-base indicators).

concepts.name: Proton transfer; strong and weak acids
concepts.description: Cambridge Supplement only (7.1): acids as proton (H⁺) donors and bases as proton acceptors; strong acids completely dissociated (HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)) and weak acids partially dissociated (CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + CH₃COO⁻(aq)); comparing strong and weak acids of the same concentration (pH, rate of reaction with magnesium or a carbonate); strength is different from concentration.

concepts.name: Acidic, basic and amphoteric oxides
concepts.description: Classifying oxides as acidic (non-metal oxides such as SO₂, SO₃, CO₂ and NO₂) or basic (metal oxides such as CuO, CaO and Na₂O), linked to the metallic or non-metallic character of the element; amphoteric oxides such as Al₂O₃ and ZnO react with both acids and bases to form a salt and water (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC Form 3).

concepts.name: Preparing soluble salts
concepts.description: Making a pure, dry soluble salt by reacting an acid with an excess of a metal, an insoluble base or an insoluble carbonate, filtering off the excess and crystallising the filtrate; making sodium, potassium and ammonium salts by titrating an acid with an alkali; choosing a method for a named salt; ZIMSEC: neutralisation and displacement (metal) methods. Cambridge 7.3; ZIMSEC Form 3.

concepts.name: Solubility rules and precipitation
concepts.description: The general solubility rules (sodium, potassium and ammonium salts and all nitrates are soluble; chlorides except silver and lead; sulfates except barium, calcium and lead; carbonates and hydroxides insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium, with calcium hydroxide slightly soluble); preparing an insoluble salt by mixing two solutions, filtering, washing and drying the precipitate (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC Form 3 precipitation); ionic equations for precipitation.

concepts.name: Hydrated salts and water of crystallisation
concepts.description: Cambridge only (7.3): hydrated and anhydrous substances; water of crystallisation in CuSO₄·5H₂O and CoCl₂·6H₂O (Supplement); the colour changes when they are heated and when water is added back; calculating the number of molecules of water of crystallisation from heating data (Supplement).

concepts.name: The Periodic Table and periodic trends
concepts.description: The Periodic Table as elements arranged in order of proton number in periods and groups; the change from metallic to non-metallic character across a period; links between group number, outer-shell electrons and ion charge, and between period number and the number of electron shells; why elements in a group react similarly; using position to predict properties; Cambridge Supplement: identifying trends in a group from data. Cambridge 8.1; ZIMSEC Form 3 periodic trends.

concepts.name: Group I: the alkali metals
concepts.description: Cambridge only (8.2): lithium, sodium and potassium as soft, reactive metals; general trends down the group (melting point decreases, density increases, reactivity increases); reactions with water to form a hydroxide and hydrogen, with observations and equations; predicting the properties of rubidium and caesium. ZIMSEC Forms 3-4 study Groups II and VII instead.

concepts.name: Group II: magnesium, calcium and barium
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 3 only: Group II elements have two outer-shell electrons and form 2+ ions; reactions of magnesium, calcium and barium with oxygen and with water (magnesium with steam), with observations and equations; reactivity increasing down the group; the oxides and hydroxides as bases.

concepts.name: Group VII: the halogens
concepts.description: Chlorine, bromine and iodine as diatomic non-metals; their appearance at room temperature (pale yellow-green gas, red-brown liquid, grey-black solid); trends down the group (density increases, reactivity decreases; ZIMSEC also colour and volatility); displacement reactions of halogens with halide ions and their explanation; predicting the properties of fluorine and astatine; safe handling (chlorine and bromine are toxic). Cambridge 8.3; ZIMSEC Form 3 group trends.

concepts.name: Transition elements
concepts.description: Transition elements as metals with high densities and melting points that form coloured compounds and act as catalysts (as elements and in compounds); Cambridge Supplement: ions with variable oxidation numbers such as iron(II) and iron(III); ZIMSEC Form 4: copper, iron, manganese, cobalt, chromium, nickel and vanadium, colours of ions such as Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺, Cr³⁺, MnO₄⁻, Cr₂O₇²⁻ and CrO₄²⁻, and their industrial and biological importance (catalysts, alloys, iron in haemoglobin).

concepts.name: The noble gases
concepts.description: Group VIII (0) noble gases as unreactive, monatomic gases, explained by their full outer shells (Cambridge 8.5); uses linked to their unreactivity and low density (argon in light bulbs and welding, helium in balloons, neon in advertising signs), which ZIMSEC teaches with the separation of air (Form 4).

concepts.name: Properties of metals and non-metals
concepts.description: Comparing the physical properties of metals and non-metals (thermal and electrical conductivity, malleability and ductility, melting and boiling points, density, lustre) and explaining the differences by structure and bonding; general chemical properties of metals: reactions with oxygen, with cold water or steam and with dilute acids; metal oxides as bases. Cambridge 9.1; ZIMSEC Form 3.

concepts.name: Uses of metals
concepts.description: Linking uses of metals to their properties: aluminium for aircraft (low density), overhead power cables (low density, good conductor) and food containers (resists corrosion), and copper for electrical wiring (good conductor, ductile) (Cambridge Core); ZIMSEC Form 4: wider uses of metals mined in Zimbabwe, such as iron and steel in construction, platinum-group metals in catalytic converters, gold in jewellery and electronics, nickel and chromium in stainless steel and lithium in rechargeable batteries.

concepts.name: Alloys
concepts.description: Alloys as mixtures of a metal with other elements: brass (copper and zinc), bronze (copper and tin), steel and stainless steel (iron with carbon, chromium and nickel) and duralumin (an aluminium alloy, ZIMSEC); alloys are harder and stronger than the pure metals, explained by different-sized atoms stopping layers sliding (Cambridge Supplement); uses such as stainless-steel cutlery; recognising alloys in particle diagrams. Cambridge 9.3; ZIMSEC Form 4 (alloys of copper, iron and aluminium).

concepts.name: The reactivity series and displacement
concepts.description: The order K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, (C), Zn, Fe, (H), Cu, Ag, Au; reactions of metals with cold water, steam and dilute hydrochloric acid explained by their position; deducing an order of reactivity from experimental results; displacement reactions with solutions of metal ions (for example zinc in copper(II) sulfate) explained by the tendency to form positive ions (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC Form 3); Cambridge Supplement: aluminium's protective oxide layer; ZIMSEC: using the series to explain cells, electroplating and metal extraction.

concepts.name: Rusting and its prevention
concepts.description: Cambridge only (9.5): iron and steel rust to hydrated iron(III) oxide only when both water and oxygen are present; barrier methods (painting, greasing, plastic coating) keep out water and oxygen; Supplement: galvanising with zinc as both a barrier and sacrificial protection, explained by the reactivity series and electron loss; experiments on the conditions for rusting (a practical-paper context).

concepts.name: Extracting metals and the blast furnace
concepts.description: How easily a metal is extracted depends on its reactivity: very reactive metals by electrolysis, metals below carbon by reduction with carbon, unreactive metals such as gold found native; the blast furnace for iron from haematite: burning coke, forming carbon monoxide, reducing iron(III) oxide, decomposing limestone and forming slag (symbol equations are Cambridge Supplement). Cambridge 9.6; ZIMSEC Form 4 extraction of metals (Zimbabwe's iron and steel industry).

concepts.name: Extracting aluminium by electrolysis
concepts.description: Bauxite as the main ore and electrolysis as the extraction method (Cambridge Core); Cambridge Supplement: electrolysis of purified aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite (lower operating temperature, better conductivity), carbon anodes burning away in the oxygen formed and needing replacement, and the electrode half-equations. ZIMSEC Form 4 scope chart lists the electrolytic production of aluminium with copper (to confirm).

concepts.name: Mineral ores and their composition
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 4 only: what makes a rock an ore; the main ores of iron (haematite, magnetite), copper (chalcopyrite, also called copper pyrites), nickel, the platinum-group metals of the Great Dyke, lithium (for example petalite and spodumene) and gold (native gold); calculating the percentage of a metal in an ore.

concepts.name: Processing minerals: value addition and beneficiation
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 4 only: outline stages in processing ores (crushing and grinding, concentration such as froth flotation, roasting or smelting, refining) for copper, nickel, platinum and gold, including electrolytic refining; value addition and beneficiation (processing minerals in Zimbabwe rather than exporting raw ore) and their economic benefits; safety and environmental issues of mining and processing.

concepts.name: Air pollution: sources, effects and control
concepts.description: Composition of clean, dry air (about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, the rest mainly noble gases and carbon dioxide); sources and effects of carbon monoxide, particulates, sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen; acid rain and photochemical smog; reducing pollution with catalytic converters, low-sulfur fuels and flue-gas desulfurisation with calcium oxide; Cambridge Supplement: how oxides of nitrogen form in engines and are removed (2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂); ZIMSEC Form 4: industrial, exhaust and domestic sources, health hazards and pollution control. Cambridge 10.3.

concepts.name: Greenhouse gases and climate change
concepts.description: Carbon dioxide (complete combustion of carbon-containing fuels) and methane (decomposing vegetation, digestion in livestock) as greenhouse gases; Cambridge Supplement: how they absorb and re-emit thermal energy so that less escapes to space; global warming and climate change; ways to reduce them (planting trees, reducing livestock farming, burning less fossil fuel, using hydrogen and renewable energy such as solar and hydroelectric power); photosynthesis removing carbon dioxide (word equation; Cambridge Supplement symbol equation). Cambridge 10.3; ZIMSEC Form 3 effects of waste.

concepts.name: The ozone layer
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (effects of waste and pollution): how the ozone layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation; its depletion by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) from old refrigerants and aerosols; effects on health and crops (skin cancer, eye damage); protecting it by phasing out CFCs and using safer alternatives.

concepts.name: Water: tests, sources and pollutants
concepts.description: Chemical tests for water with anhydrous copper(II) sulfate (white to blue) and anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride (blue to pink); testing whether water is pure from its melting and boiling points; why distilled water is used in experiments; substances in natural water (dissolved oxygen, metal compounds, plastics, sewage, microbes, nitrates and phosphates) and whether each is beneficial or harmful (Cambridge 10.1); ZIMSEC Form 3: water from dams, boreholes, rivers and rain compared by colour, smell and pH, and eutrophication (Cambridge does not require its details).

concepts.name: Hard and soft water
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 3 only: hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium ions; testing hardness by how easily soap lathers and by boiling and examining the residue; effects of hard water (scale in kettles, geysers, boilers and pipes; scum with soap); removing scale with acids such as vinegar or lemon juice; temporary and permanent hardness and simple ways of softening water.

concepts.name: Treatment of the water supply
concepts.description: Stages in treating water for towns: sedimentation and filtration (sand filters) to remove solids, carbon to remove tastes and smells, and chlorination to kill microbes (Cambridge Core); ZIMSEC Form 4: flocculation with aluminium sulfate, the roles of aluminium sulfate and chlorine, and problems in water treatment (polluted sources, cost of chemicals); treating drinking water at home. Cambridge 10.1.

concepts.name: Types and sources of waste
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 3 only: solid, liquid and gaseous waste; biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste; household and industrial sources (food waste, waste gases, gold processing, oils from soap making, tyre manufacture, cement dust); identifying industrial wastes; ways of controlling waste.

concepts.name: Waste disposal, reuse and recycling
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 4 only: incineration, landfills and the activated sludge treatment of sewage, with the advantages and disadvantages of each; composting and biogas digesters; reducing, reusing and recycling waste (paper, metals, glass and plastics).

concepts.name: Herbs in health and agriculture
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 4 only: plants used traditionally in Zimbabwe in health care and agriculture (for example herbal teas and natural pest repellents), the idea that their effects come from chemicals they contain, and the advantages (availability, low cost, indigenous knowledge) and disadvantages (uncertain dosage, side effects, toxicity, lack of testing) of using them. Never present a herb as a proven cure.

concepts.name: Types of fuels
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 3 only: fuels classified as solid (wood, charcoal, coal, coke), liquid (petrol, diesel, paraffin, ethanol, biodiesel) and gaseous (natural gas, LPG, biogas); fossil and renewable fuels; the properties of a good fuel; fuels used in Zimbabwean homes and industry and their effects on health and the environment.

concepts.name: Fuel efficiency and heating values
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 4 only: determining the heating value of a fuel by experiment (energy released per gram, heating water with a spirit burner or candle; q = mcΔT); explaining why some fuels release more energy per gram or burn more cleanly than others (composition, moisture content, complete and incomplete combustion); choosing fuels by heating value, cost, availability and pollution.

concepts.name: Fossil fuels and the fractional distillation of crude oil
concepts.description: Coal, natural gas (mainly methane) and petroleum as fossil fuels; hydrocarbons; petroleum as a mixture of hydrocarbons separated into fractions by fractional distillation; how chain length, volatility, boiling point and viscosity change from the bottom to the top of the column; uses of refinery gas, petrol, naphtha, kerosene (paraffin), diesel, fuel oil, lubricating oil and bitumen. Cambridge 11.3; ZIMSEC Form 3 production of fuels (outline).

concepts.name: Fuels from coal, wood and biomass
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 3 only: destructive distillation of coal (coke, coal gas, coal tar, ammoniacal liquor) and of wood (charcoal and other products); biogas (mainly methane) from the anaerobic digestion of animal and plant waste in digesters; biodiesel from plant oils such as jatropha oil; advantages and disadvantages of these fuels.

concepts.name: Organic formulae and homologous series
concepts.description: Molecular, structural, displayed and general formulae; functional groups; homologous series (alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, alkenes CₙH₂ₙ, alcohols CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH, carboxylic acids CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH) and their characteristics (same functional group and general formula, successive members differ by CH₂, trend in physical properties, similar chemical properties: Cambridge Supplement); saturated and unsaturated compounds. Cambridge 11.1; ZIMSEC Form 3 (classifying hydrocarbons, alcohols and carboxylic acids with up to six carbon atoms).

concepts.name: Naming organic compounds
concepts.description: Naming and drawing alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids and recognising their family from -ane, -ene, -ol and -oic acid endings or from formulae (Cambridge Core: methane, ethane, ethene, ethanol, ethanoic acid and the products of their reactions; Cambridge Supplement: unbranched compounds with up to four carbon atoms, including but-1-ene, but-2-ene, propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol, and esters; ZIMSEC Form 3: systematic names for compounds with up to six carbon atoms).

concepts.name: Structural isomerism
concepts.description: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae; Cambridge Supplement: C₄H₁₀ (butane and methylpropane) and C₄H₈ (but-1-ene and but-2-ene); ZIMSEC Form 4: drawing and naming the structural isomers of alkanes with up to six carbon atoms (for example the five isomers of C₆H₁₄).

concepts.name: Alkanes
concepts.description: Alkanes as saturated hydrocarbons with only single carbon-carbon bonds; generally unreactive apart from combustion (complete and incomplete) and substitution with chlorine; Cambridge Supplement: substitution reactions and the photochemical monosubstitution of alkanes by chlorine in ultraviolet light; ZIMSEC Form 4: methane with chlorine in ultraviolet light and in the dark. Cambridge 11.4.

concepts.name: Cracking
concepts.description: Breaking long-chain alkanes into shorter alkanes, alkenes and hydrogen using a high temperature and a catalyst; why cracking is needed (demand for petrol and for alkenes to make polymers and ethanol); balancing cracking equations; the school experiment of cracking liquid paraffin or cooking oil over a hot catalyst and testing the gas with bromine water (ZIMSEC). Cambridge 11.5; ZIMSEC Form 4.

concepts.name: Alkenes and addition reactions
concepts.description: Alkenes as unsaturated hydrocarbons with a carbon-carbon double bond; the aqueous bromine test (orange to colourless) to tell alkenes from alkanes; combustion; addition reactions of alkenes with bromine, with hydrogen using a nickel catalyst (hardening vegetable oils to make margarine) and with steam using an acid catalyst (making ethanol), and drawing the products (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC Form 4, as shown by ethene). Cambridge 11.5.

concepts.name: Making ethanol
concepts.description: Fermentation of glucose by yeast at 25-35 °C without oxygen, and the catalytic addition of steam to ethene at 300 °C and 60 atm with an acid catalyst (Cambridge Core); advantages and disadvantages of each method (Cambridge Supplement); ZIMSEC Form 4: conditions for fermentation, industrial ethanol from sugar cane, and traditional fermentation such as brewing indigenous beer from sorghum, rapoko or maize.

concepts.name: Properties and uses of ethanol
concepts.description: Combustion of ethanol and its uses as a solvent and a fuel (Cambridge Core); ZIMSEC Form 4: solubility in water and boiling point, oxidation to ethanoic acid, dehydration to ethene, the test with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) (orange to green), uses in fuel blends with petrol, perfumes and drinks, and the social effects of alcohol misuse. Cambridge 11.6.

concepts.name: Carboxylic acids and esters
concepts.description: Ethanoic acid as a weak acid that reacts with metals, bases and carbonates to form ethanoate salts (Cambridge Core); making ethanoic acid by oxidising ethanol with acidified potassium manganate(VII) or by bacteria in vinegar making (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC Form 4); esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol using an acid catalyst and naming esters (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC); uses of ethanoic acid and esters in perfumes, flavourings and food preservation (ZIMSEC). Cambridge 11.7.

concepts.name: Soaps and saponification
concepts.description: ZIMSEC Form 4 only: making soap by heating fats or oils with sodium hydroxide (saponification) to give soap and glycerol; the structure of a soap particle (a water-attracting ionic head and an oil-attracting hydrocarbon tail) and how soap removes grease; making soap safely in the laboratory; soap forming scum in hard water.

concepts.name: Addition polymers and plastics
concepts.description: Polymers as large molecules built from many monomers; addition polymerisation of ethene to poly(ethene) (polythene); plastics are made from polymers; disposal problems (non-biodegradable in landfill, building up in rivers and oceans, toxic gases when burned) (Cambridge Core); Cambridge Supplement: repeat units and deducing the polymer from the alkene and the alkene from the polymer (for example poly(propene) and poly(chloroethene)); uses of synthetic polymers (ZIMSEC Form 4). Cambridge 11.8.

concepts.name: Condensation polymers: nylon and polyesters
concepts.description: Condensation polymerisation, in which a small molecule such as water is lost as each link forms: polyamides such as nylon from a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine, and polyesters such as PET (Terylene) from a dicarboxylic acid and a diol; amide and ester linkages; drawing repeat units as block diagrams; differences between addition and condensation polymerisation; PET can be turned back into its monomers and re-polymerised; uses. Cambridge Supplement (11.8); ZIMSEC Form 4.

concepts.name: Natural polymers: proteins and starch
concepts.description: Proteins as natural polyamides formed from amino acids (general structure; amide (peptide) linkages) (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC Form 4); ZIMSEC Form 4 only: starch as a natural polymer of glucose, naming the linkages, deducing monomers from polymers and the reverse, and the acid hydrolysis of starch and proteins (products can be identified by chromatography). Cambridge 11.8.

concepts.name: Apparatus and measurement
concepts.description: Naming and choosing apparatus to measure time, temperature, mass, volume and length (stop-watch, thermometer, balance, burette, volumetric pipette, measuring cylinder, gas syringe, ruler); using them correctly; reading scales to the nearest half division and recording to a suitable precision; advantages and disadvantages of methods and apparatus. Cambridge 12.1 and the practical papers; ZIMSEC Form 3 measuring instruments.

concepts.name: Planning investigations: variables, control and safety
concepts.description: Identifying independent, dependent and controlled variables; planning a fair test with a suitable range and number of values and repeats; choosing apparatus and describing a method step by step; identifying hazards (corrosive, flammable, toxic, oxidising, harmful to the environment) and safety precautions; making and testing predictions. Assessed in Cambridge Papers 5 and 6 (section 4 of the syllabus) and in ZIMSEC Paper 3 and school-based assessment.

concepts.name: Recording, presenting and evaluating data
concepts.description: Recording results in tables (quantity / unit headings, consistent precision); plotting graphs (labelled axes with units, sensible scales, best-fit lines or curves); reading values by interpolation and extrapolation; gradients (Cambridge Extended: tangent to a curve); means; significant figures; identifying anomalous results and sources of error; suggesting improvements and drawing conclusions justified by the data.

concepts.name: Separating mixtures
concepts.description: Key terms (solvent, solute, solution, saturated solution, residue, filtrate); separating and purifying with a suitable solvent, filtration, evaporation, crystallisation and simple distillation; choosing a method from given properties such as solubility and boiling point; everyday examples (purifying rock salt, sand filters, obtaining pure water). Cambridge 12.4 and 12.1; ZIMSEC Form 3 separation techniques.

concepts.name: Fractional distillation and steam distillation
concepts.description: Fractional distillation of miscible liquids with different boiling points (for example ethanol and water; links to crude oil and liquid air): the apparatus, how the fractionating column works and reading the thermometer (Cambridge 12.4; ZIMSEC Form 4); ZIMSEC Form 4 only: steam distillation to extract heat-sensitive oils from plant material for perfumes and flavours.

concepts.name: Chromatography
concepts.description: Paper chromatography to separate soluble coloured substances (inks, food colourings, plant pigments): setting up (pencil base line above the solvent level) and interpreting chromatograms to identify substances and judge purity (Cambridge Core); Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC Form 4); locating agents for colourless substances (Cambridge Supplement); thin-layer chromatography (ZIMSEC). Cambridge 12.3.

concepts.name: Purity: melting and boiling points
concepts.description: Pure substances have sharp, fixed melting and boiling points; impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range, and raise the boiling point; using melting and boiling point data to identify substances and judge their purity; why purity matters in foods, medicines and drugs. Cambridge 12.4; ZIMSEC Form 4 (effects of impurities on melting and boiling points).

concepts.name: Acid-base titration technique
concepts.description: Carrying out an acid-base titration with a volumetric pipette, burette, conical flask and a suitable indicator (methyl orange or thymolphthalein in Cambridge; phenolphthalein is also common); recognising the end-point; reading the burette to 0.05 cm³; rough and accurate titres, concordant results and the mean titre; completing a titration table; using titration to prepare a soluble salt. Cambridge 12.2; ZIMSEC Form 4 volumetric analysis.

concepts.name: Tests for cations
concepts.description: Identifying aqueous cations from the precipitates formed with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia (colour, and whether they dissolve in excess): Al³⁺, NH₄⁺, Cr³⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺ and Zn²⁺ for both boards, Ca²⁺ for Cambridge, and Mg²⁺ and Pb²⁺ for ZIMSEC; Cambridge: flame tests for Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Ba²⁺ and Cu²⁺; ionic equations for the precipitates. Cambridge 12.5; ZIMSEC Form 4 qualitative analysis.

concepts.name: Tests for anions
concepts.description: Tests for carbonate (dilute acid, then carbon dioxide turns limewater milky), chloride, bromide and iodide (dilute nitric acid then aqueous silver nitrate: white, cream and yellow precipitates), nitrate (aqueous sodium hydroxide and aluminium foil, warmed: ammonia given off), sulfate (dilute nitric acid then aqueous barium nitrate: white precipitate) and sulfite (decolourises acidified potassium manganate(VII); Cambridge only); ZIMSEC lists Cl⁻, I⁻, NO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻ and CO₃²⁻. Cambridge 12.5; ZIMSEC Form 4.

concepts.name: Tests for gases
concepts.description: Tests and results for ammonia (turns damp red litmus blue), carbon dioxide (turns limewater milky), chlorine (bleaches damp litmus), hydrogen (pops with a lighted splint), oxygen (relights a glowing splint) and sulfur dioxide (turns acidified potassium manganate(VII) from purple to colourless), and which reactions give each gas. Cambridge 12.5; ZIMSEC Form 4 qualitative analysis.
